title: Comparative Phenotypic and Molecular Characterisation of Feline Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma Cell Lines Reveals Marked Biological Heterogeneity.
abstract: Feline oral squamous cell carcinoma (FOSCC) is the most common oral malignancy, characterised by aggressive local invasion, frequent bone involvement, and poor prognosis. The limited availability of well-characterised in vitro models has hindered the understanding of tumour heterogeneity and invasive behaviour. This study aimed to establish and comparatively characterise a panel of FOSCC cell lines derived from tumours with and without documented bone invasion to identify intrinsic biological differences. Four FOSCC cell lines were evaluated for epithelial identity, growth kinetics, clonogenicity, migratory capacity and chemosensitivity. All cell lines retained epithelial characteristics, with consistent expression of epithelial markers; however, variation in cytokeratin-19 and vimentin suggested phenotypic heterogeneity and partial epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity. The cell lines demonstrated distinct proliferation rates, doubling times, and clonogenic capacities. Morphologically, these cells displayed varying degrees of peripheral filopodial activity. Functional assays further revealed substantial migratory capacity under both serum-supplemented and serum-free conditions, with differences across cell lines. Chemosensitivity profiling showed heterogeneous responses to targeted and cytotoxic agents, highlighting cell line-specific differences in drug susceptibility and potential intrinsic drug responsiveness. These findings demonstrate that FOSCC cell lines possess distinct biological properties consistent with phenotypic differences. The observed heterogeneity underscores the potential relevance of tumour origin in shaping functional behaviour and highlights the value of using multiple, well-characterised cell line models to better represent disease diversity. This study provides a comprehensive comparative characterisation of four FOSCC cell lines, including a newly established model, and establishes a baseline resource for future mechanistic and translational investigations in feline and comparative oncology.

title: Successful use of insect-based (Hermetia illucens) diet in dogs with food-responsive enteropathy.
abstract: Objective Diet is an integral component of the management of chronic enteropathy in dogs. The role of insect-based diets in this disease remains unknown. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of an insect-based (Hermetia illucens) diet in dogs with presumed food-responsive enteropathy. Methods Twenty-seven client-owned dogs with evidence of chronic enteropathy, in which diet was required as sole management, were enrolled onto this prospective, uncontrolled diet trial. Canine inflammatory bowel disease activity index, faecal score, body condition score and body weight (kg) were recorded pre-enrolment (T 0 ). Dogs were exclusively fed insect diet and reassessed at 14 (T 1 ), 30 (T 2 ) and 90 (T 3 ) days. Dogs remained in the study if responding and exited the study at various times for additional investigations or alternative treatment(s) if not responding. Comparisons were made within responders over time and between responders and non-responders at T 0 . Data are expressed as median (range). Results Twenty-seven dogs were recruited; seven cases were withdrawn, leaving 20 dogs for analysis. Fourteen/20 dogs (70%) were classified as responders with a decrease in median faecal score from 6.25 (5 to 7) at T 0 to 2 (2 to 5) at T 1 and a median decrease in canine inflammatory bowel disease activity index from 8 (5 to 14) at T 0 to 1 (0 to 5) at T 1 . All responders had adequate control at day 90 (T 3 ), with a median faecal score of 2 (2 to 5) and a median canine inflammatory bowel disease activity index of 0 (0 to 3). Clinical significance Insect diet improved clinical signs in 70% of chronic enteropathy dogs and could represent another dietary option in the management of this disease.

title: Intraoperative cholangiography during open cholecystectomy in 73 dogs with benign gallbladder disease.
abstract: Objective To evaluate intraoperative cholangiography (IOC) during open cholecystectomy in dogs with benign gallbladder disease, including cases with preoperative common bile duct (CBD) obstruction, and to describe the short-term outcomes. Study design Retrospective case series. Animals A total of 73 client-owned dogs. Methods Medical records (2014-2022) were reviewed. All dogs underwent open cholecystectomy, bile duct flushing (BDF) with saline, and IOC under subtraction fluoroscopy. Cholangiograms were assessed for complete CBD obstruction (no duodenal passage), partial obstruction (CBD filling defects indicating retained debris), and filling defects in hepatic ducts. Perioperative mortality (≤14 days) and post-discharge findings during 3 months of follow-up were recorded. Results IOC was evaluable in 72 of 73 dogs; assessment was precluded by catheter perforation in one dog. Complete CBD obstruction was identified in 12.5% (9/72). Partial obstruction with retained debris occurred in 20.8% (15/72); debris migrated to transiently obstruct the distal CBD during contrast injection in four of 15. Among the 66 dogs in which IOC opacified the right and left hepatic ducts, seven (10.6%) had filling defects in the hepatic ducts. One dog developed suspected contrast-associated shock that resolved with treatment. Perioperative mortality was 6.8% (5/73) in the total cohort; 0% (0/29) in dogs without jaundice, and 11.4% (5/44) in dogs with jaundice. Among 61 dogs with follow-up, no deaths occurred within 3 months. Conclusion During open cholecystectomy, IOC frequently identified retained debris and other biliary abnormalities. Clinical significance IOC may be a useful adjunct to BDF when CBD or hepatic duct obstruction or retained debris is suspected. Routine IOC may improve surgical outcomes, particularly in dogs with preoperative CBD obstruction.

title: Skeletal modifications after transpelvic urethrostomy as treatment for urethral stricture in a three-month-old cat.
abstract: Objective To describe the occurrence, management, and long-term outcome of bilateral lateral displacement of the ischial tuberosities following transpelvic urethrostomy (TPU) performed to treat intrapelvic urethral rupture and obstruction in a skeletally immature cat. Animals One 3-month-old male domestic short-haired cat. Study design Case report. Methods A young cat with intrapelvic urethral rupture secondary to repeated unsuccessful urethral catheterizations was initially managed conservatively and subsequently underwent perineal urethrostomy, which failed due to recurrent intrapelvic urethral stenosis. Transpelvic urethrostomy was then performed as a salvage procedure. Clinical follow-up included serial physical examinations, radiography, computed tomography (CT), orthopedic assessment, and owner-completed functional questionnaires over a three-year period. Results The cat regained voluntary urination within 12 h postoperatively and remained continent. Follow-up radiographs at 2 months revealed bilateral lateral displacement of the ischial tuberosities, with pelvic width measuring 46.2 mm at the iliac wings and 55.7 mm at the ischial tuberosities, compared with a pelvic length of 79.6 mm. At 3 years, CT measurements showed dorsal acetabular rim angles of 16.9°-18.1° and an acetabular angle of 45°. Functional assessment demonstrated minimal musculoskeletal pain (feline musculoskeletal pain index [FMPI] = 2/72) and negligible disability (average disability score [ADS] = 0.75/16), with preserved locomotor function. Conclusion Transpelvic urethrostomy can be a feasible and effective surgical option for managing intrapelvic urethral rupture in skeletally immature cats. Although pelvic morphological alterations may occur following caudal pelvic symphyseal release, these changes were not associated with functional impairment in this case, highlighting the potential role of TPU as a salvage procedure in selected juvenile feline patients.

title: Sepsis and elevated creatinine predict poor outcomes in uncomplicated canine pyometra, and empirically prescribed antibiotics do not match bacterial susceptibility or improve survival.
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: Objective To identify variables associated with prolonged hospitalization or nonsurvival in the surgical management of pyometra in dogs and to report uterine bacterial susceptibility in comparison with empirically prescribed antibiotics. Methods Retrospective study of dogs that underwent ovariohysterectomy for management of pyometra at 8 tertiary referral centers between December 1, 2008, and December 31, 2023. Data collected included signalment, preoperative/operative data, antibiotic utilization, and clinical follow-up. Results 625 dogs met inclusion criteria. Forty dogs (6.4%) experienced major short-term complications, and 604 dogs (96.6%) survived to discharge. Elevated preoperative creatinine concentration and sepsis increased the risk of nonsurvival. Survival to discharge did not differ between nonseptic dogs that received pre- or intraoperative antibiotics and those that did not. Sepsis, elevated creatinine, and interaction between elevated creatinine and altered mentation increased hospitalization duration. At least 1 inappropriate outpatient antibiotic was prescribed in 34.4% (116 of 337) of cases; most dogs that received inappropriate antibiotics were empirically prescribed amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (102 of 116 [87.9%]). Conclusions Surgical management of pyometra in the tertiary referral setting had a good prognosis regardless of prescribed antibiotic bacterial susceptibility. Elevated creatinine and/or sepsis increased risk of mortality and prolonged hospitalization. The use of pre- and intraoperative antibiotics in nonseptic dogs was not associated with outcome. Clinical relevance There was no clear clinical benefit of antibiotic use in the surgical management of pyometra in nonseptic dogs. If empiric antibiotics are indicated, the bacterial susceptibility profile of this patient population suggests a high likelihood of resistance to amoxicillin-clavulanic acid.

title: Cefovecin selects for higher-level and more persistent antimicrobial resistance among gastrointestinal Escherichia coli in some cats compared to amoxicillin-clavulanic acid in an observational longitudinal study.
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: Objective This observational study compared the development and persistence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in feline microbiota following treatment with cefovecin or amoxicillin-clavulanic acid. Methods Cats treated with cefovecin or amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, at the attending veterinarian's discretion, were recruited from multiple sources between December 2022 and May 2024. Fecal samples were collected on the first day of treatment and 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, and 12 weeks afterward. Samples were cultured for Escherichia coli, Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion was performed, and isolates with decreased cefovecin susceptibility were enumerated. Samples were tested for AMR genes with a targeted deep amplicon sequencing panel. The proportions of nonsusceptible isolates were compared across time and treatments. Results 9 cats treated with cefovecin and 10 cats treated with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid were included. Both groups developed ampicillin-resistant E coli, which persisted longer in the cefovecin group. There were significantly greater odds of recovering E coli not susceptible to amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (OR, 72; 95% CI, 5.4 to 980), ceftriaxone (OR, 930; 95% CI, 81 to 11,000), and cefoxitin (OR, 46, 95% CI, 1.7 to 1,200) in the cefovecin group, driven by 1 cefovecin-treated cat shedding resistant E coli for weeks 1 through 4. Conclusions A minority of cats may shed E coli resistant to β-lactams following cefovecin treatment, and the risk of AMR is likely lower after amoxicillin-clavulanic acid treatment. Clinical relevance Since cats are commonly treated with cefovecin, some treated cats shedding high-level β-lactam-resistant E coli may pose a threat to feline and human health. Using amoxicillin-clavulanic acid instead may minimize resistance.

title: BRAFV595E mutation detected across the disease spectrum from non-neoplastic urothelium to invasive urothelial carcinoma in dogs.
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: Objective The goal was to determine the presence of a driver mutation in dogs with and without detectable cancer to set the stage for future cancer prevention research exploiting processes that inhibit cancer development in the presence of such mutations. The objective was to detect the v-raf murine sarcoma viral oncogene homolog B (BRAF) mutation BRAFV595E across the disease spectrum from non-neoplastic urothelium to invasive urothelial carcinoma (UC) in dogs. Methods Scottish Terriers ≥ 6 years old with no outward evidence of urinary disease (n = 120) were screened for UC by urinalysis, urinary tract ultrasonography, follow-up cystoscopic biopsy, and necropsy when possible. Initial results were published in 2022. Extended follow-up is presented here. The BRAFV595E mutation was detected in urine sediment by droplet digital PCR and in bladder tissues by immunohistochemistry. Results For 120 dogs screened, biopsy-confirmed UC was found in 41 dogs including 31 high-grade UC, 6 low-grade UC, 1 carcinoma in situ, and 3 dysplasias that progressed to high-grade UC. The BRAFV595E mutation was found in the urine of 23 of 26 dogs with high-grade UC, 4 of 5 dogs with low-grade UC, 2 of 3 dogs with dysplasia, and 12 of 66 dogs with no UC detected over a median of 14 months of follow-up (range, 4 to 71 months). The BRAFV595E mutation was detected in UC and non-neoplastic urothelium by immunohistochemistry. Conclusions The BRAFV595E mutation is present in various stages of canine UC and non-neoplastic urothelium. This knowledge will contribute to future cancer prevention research. Clinical relevance Urothelial carcinoma screening should be implemented for Scottish Terriers and potentially dogs in other high-risk breeds. Biopsy and standardized imaging remain essential in UC management.

title: Assessment of Clinical and Immunological Factors of Local Recurrence in Canine Soft Tissue Sarcoma.
abstract: Canine soft tissue sarcomas (STSs) are locally invasive tumours, making local recurrence a major clinical challenge. Time to recurrence (TTR) and associated immune factors remain poorly characterized. This study aimed to characterize the immune microenvironment of canine STS and identify factors associated with TTR. Medical records from 27 dogs with STS that recurred after surgery were reviewed. Histopathological, transcriptomic, and immunological analyses were performed in a tissue-available subcohort of 20 dogs. Immune-related gene expression was characterized using the NanoString canine IO panel. Tumour-infiltrating immune cells and tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) were assessed immunohistochemically using CD3, CD20, and FoxP3. Associations with TTR were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards models and log-rank tests. Median TTR was 358 days. Age and tumour location were associated with TTR in univariable analyses of the full cohort, but neither age nor the overall location effect remained significant when analysed together. Higher NOD2 expression and Cluster 1 assignment were associated with shorter TTR across exploratory multivariable models. Cluster 1 tumours exhibited abundant lymphocyte infiltration and enrichment of immunosuppressive pathways, whereas Cluster 2 tumours demonstrated lower immune infiltration and proinflammatory signatures. TLS-positive tumours had greater lymphocyte infiltration, with FoxP3+ cells accumulated within TLSs. Paired recurrent tumours contained significantly more large TLSs than primary tumours. Higher NOD2 expression and an immunologically active but suppressed tumour phenotype were associated with shorter TTR, whereas the association with anatomical location was model-dependent. Regulatory T cells and TLSs may contribute to the immune landscape associated with local recurrence and warrant further investigation as potential therapeutic targets.
